We introduce MaskedVGGT, which freezes a strong pretrained 2D encoder and pretrains only an added, randomly initialized multi-view transformer, focusing on learning interactions across views. MaskedVGGT pretrains the multi-view transformer through masked self-distillation without annotations: a student predicts targets at masked locations based on complete anchor views and heavily masked remaining views, while an exponential-moving-average teacher provides prediction targets based on unmasked inputs. In experiments across model sizes up to 1B parameters, MaskedVGGT pretraining followed by fine-tuning outperforms single-stage supervised VGGT-$Ω$ training with the same training data, model architecture, and total number of optimization updates. MaskedVGGT also outperforms E-RayZer, CroCo, MuM, and Muskie, providing evidence for the effectiveness of building multi-view pretraining on strong 2D representations. Finally, extending pretraining with additional unlabeled videos further improves generalization, and the learned representations transfer to diverse downstream tasks. These results demonstrate an effective division of learning: reuse strong image representations from 2D pretraining and learn cross-view interactions from unlabeled multi-view data without relying on geometric annotations.
comment: The submitting author requests standard withdrawal after reconsidering the timing of public dissemination of this work
♻ ☆ Where Compute Matters: Heterogeneous Attention for Efficient Video Diffusion
Olga Zatsarynna, Denis Korzhenkov, Juergen Gall, Amir Habibian, Mohsen Ghafoorian
Efficient video generation requires reducing the quadratic cost of self-attention over long spatiotemporal token sequences. Denoising difficulty varies across video regions and evolves throughout generation, motivating an adaptive allocation of global context. We introduce HetA-DiT, a heterogeneous attention mechanism that routes uncertain tokens through global attention and processes more reliable tokens with local attention. A lightweight uncertainty branch is trained with an uncertainty-aware distribution-matching objective. At inference, its preceding-step predictions are shared across attention heads and reused across blocks, without an additional Transformer evaluation. We evaluate DMD-distilled Wan2.2-5B, Wan2.1-1.3B and Wan2.1-14B models. VBench across all three models, together with VBench2.0 and human preference evaluations on 5B, shows that HetA achieves a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off while routing only approximately 20\% of tokens through global attention. Across Wan2.1-1.3B and Wan2.2-5B/14B benchmarks on A100, HetA achieves up to 3.78x self-attention and 2.23x Transformer-block speedups over dense FlashAttention. Complete-denoising speedups grow with model size and sampling schedule, with composed runtime measurements projecting up to 2.06x for a 14B expert with 50-step sampling.
♻ ☆ Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting
Amani Aifi, Wassim Bouachir, Ahmed Zgaren, Nizar Bouguila
We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2027 IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027). Code: https://github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count
♻ ☆ Wall-to-wall maps of canopy height and aboveground carbon across the Atlantic Forest
Matheus Pinheiro Ferreira, Thiago Carmuega Rabaçal, Giulio Brossi Santoro, Giovanna de Andrade Ferreira, Rodrigo Costa Pinto, Danilo R. A. de Almeida, Paulo Guilherme Molin, Catherine Torres de Almeida, Angélica F. Resende, Vinicius Castro Souza, Marcelo Antonio Pinho Ferreira, Cássio Toledo, Eben North Broadbent, Angelica Almeyda Zambrano, Laura Simões, Juliano van Melis, Ricardo Ribeiro Rodrigues, Pedro H. S. Brancalion
Global canopy height maps are increasingly used to estimate forest carbon, yet their regional accuracy is rarely tested. We present wall-to-wall maps of canopy height (10 m) and aboveground carbon density (30 m) for the Brazilian Atlantic Forest in 2024. Height was predicted by a deep learning network fusing optical (Sentinel-2), SAR (Sentinel-1, ALOS PALSAR) and elevation (ALOS) data, trained and tested on 58,800 km$^2$ of airborne LiDAR from a statewide campaign over São Paulo state, Brazil. The mean absolute error at 10 m is 2.26 m on held-out test patches (1.90 m at 30 m) and 2.8 to 5.5 m at three independent LiDAR sites, against 4.14 m and 3.9 to 13.2 m for the Meta and World Resources Institute global product (version 2) over the same pixels. A power law fitted to 124 inventory plots converted canopy height to above ground carbon density. The remaining forest holds 1,944 TgC over 28.3 Mha. Global products therefore need local validation before use in carbon accounting.
comment: 60 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables, 1 supplementary table. Submitted to Scientific Data. Maps and code openly available via Zenodo and GitHub
♻ ☆ CONCOR: Benchmarking Contrastive Decoding for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Beyond Final-Output Performance
Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Hanjia Lyu
Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.
♻ ☆ Teaching Vision-Language Models to Decline: Support Completion Against Mirage
Alfaj Uddin Ahmed, Md. Shaown Miah, Md Arid Hasan, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown. Asadi et al. termed this failure 'mirage', where a plausible answer can be provided without being supported by the visual evidence. We trace the failure to the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it only by the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and training examples are not rewarded for declining. Our proposed method, TIDE (Training with Informative-Divergence Evidence), has two stages. The first contrasts the correct image of a question with incorrect images through an InfoNCE loss. The second completes the support. Each training question is shown with its valid image and with a blank image, an in-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain wrong image, and the target on the three counterfactuals is to decline. We show that a model that ignores the image lies in the optimal set of the standard loss and outside the optimal set of the contrast. We measure mirage with an image-aware judge that scores each response against a caption of the image the model was actually shown, so a response that flags or describes the wrong image is not counted as a mirage. On a frozen held-out test, the two stages lower the invalid-evidence mirage rate on all 15 model-seed configurations, from 0.450-0.882 for the stock models to 0.029-0.181; a text-only judge agrees on every axis. The reduction transfers zero-shot to MMStar (0.380 to 0.052) with answer accuracy within one point of the stock model. The cost is false abstention on valid images, which ranges from 0.035 to 0.250 across four seeds of one model. Ablations indicate that counterfactual images drive the effect, whereas generic refusal supervision and hard negatives do not, on each of three seeds.
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures. Includes supplementary material
♻ ☆ Medical Image Alignment Assessment as a Test of Generalist Visual Reasoning in Frontier Multimodal Models
Ross Callaghan, Niannu Gao, Hojjat Azadbakht, Hui Zhang
Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly positioned as general purpose visual reasoners as part of the quest for artificial general intelligence. A key test of this generality is whether they can perform novel visual judgments that humans can make reliably from visual evidence and task instructions, without task-specific parameter optimisation. We investigate this question through the task of medical image alignment assessment, where the goal is to establish whether there is anatomical correspondence between two images. Human visual assessment of image alignment is still the gold standard and most common approach; however, it requires trained operators and is impractical to scale for large datasets. We evaluate recent generations of MLLMs on two exemplar medical image alignment tasks, varying both prompting strategies and image-presentation methods. We compare against a locally fine-tuned MLLM and a task-specific CNN to examine the trade-off between frontier general purpose models and smaller models that require specific task optimisation but can be used locally. We show that are reaching an inflection point, where frontier MLLMs can now perform effective visual assessment of medical image alignment. Models released only a few months ago generalise poorly and, in some settings, perform barely above chance, whereas GPT-6 achieves over 85% across almost all scenarios tested. Fine-tuned local models can match or exceed frontier-model performance on the tasks on which they are trained, but transfer substantially less effectively to unseen settings. These findings identify medical image alignment as a useful test bed for generalist visual reasoning and suggest that frontier multimodal models are beginning to acquire capabilities that could support a common quality-control mechanism across heterogeneous medical-imaging pipelines.
♻ ☆ GeoMem-VLA: Internalizing 3D Scene Understanding into Temporal Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
Qinfan Zhang, Yifan Luo, Haoyuan Shi, Guanlin Liu, Han Dong, Haozhe Shan, Yong Dai, Xiancong Ren, Xiaozhu Ju
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically predict actions from current 2D observations, whereas existing 3D policies infer geometry per step without retaining it across an episode. Action generation under occlusion and across multiple stages requires a compact spatial abstraction that persists over time without reconstructing a full 3D scene at each step. Based on this insight, we introduce GeoMem-VLA, a framework that internalizes explicit 3D scene and motion supervision into learnable latent GeoPlantokens, leaving the vision-language backbone's native visual embeddings unaligned. During training, a frozen geometry teacher and demonstration trajectories supervise these tokens via an auxiliary flow-matching head over current scene point maps and future end-effector tracks. Across steps, the policy stores observation and GeoPlan representations in separate memory banks, merges similar adjacent states into event memories, and fuses retrieved history with current features to predict actions. At inference, the 3D teacher and auxiliary head are removed, and action generation relies solely on the latent GeoPlan tokens and episode memory without explicit scene reconstruction. GeoMem-VLA achieves average success rates of 98.9% on LIBERO, 91.10% and 91.24% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized settings, and 78.0% across five real-world manipulation tasks.
♻ ☆ SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape Estimation across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
Ilya Zaychuk
Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans. In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike. Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames. A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames. On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm. Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://ghostlate.github.io/SparseHPS
♻ ☆ TryOnReward: Learning Foveated Consistency for Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Virtual Try-On
Xueheng Li, Yong Liu, Xiaolong Fu, Wen Xue, Chengjun Xie, Yipeng Sun, Yan Li, Simiu Gu
Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to dress a person with the reference garment, producing visually reasonable results aligned with human preferences. Turning this preference-oriented goal into an actionable objective relies on a scoring function aligned with human taste. However, classic fidelity metrics exhibit weak correlation with human judgments, and generic VLMs fail to provide the discriminative granularity demanded by try-on quality evaluation, which hinges on faithfully preserving garment and person details. This shortcoming is further exacerbated in the reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) optimization and leads to severe reward hacking. To this end, we present TryOnReward, a fine-grained reward model tailored for VTON. Built on a vision-language backbone, it adopts a foveation calibration objective that grounds each quality dimension in the relevant region to avoid global shortcut learning. Meanwhile, TryOnReward jointly optimizes pairwise preferences and per-dimension quality scores via margin-aware supervision, leveraging both relative and absolute quality signals. For model training and evaluation, we build TryOnRank-100K, a human-annotated per-dimension rating dataset, alongside TryOn-Bench and TryOnRewardBench, two benchmarks covering diverse real scenarios. Extensive experiments confirm that our proposed TryOnReward significantly outperforms generic judges in human preference alignment, and when serving as the RFT reward function, it consistently yields human-preferred try-on results across multiple baselines.
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures
♻ ☆ Delta-SVD: Efficient Compression for Personalized Text-to-Image Models
Tangyuan Zhang, Shangyu Chen, Qixiang Chen, Junyu Yan, Jingwen Ye, Jianfei Cai
Personalizing a text-to-image diffusion model by full fine-tuning gives the strongest subject fidelity but produces a full copy of the model per subject: a thousand personalized Stable Diffusion checkpoints approach five terabytes, so storage, not compute, is what fails to scale. We present Delta-SVD, which compresses the weight change that personalization makes rather than the model. Given only a finished checkpoint and its base, it takes a truncated SVD of each layer's weight delta and keeps the few components that carry its spectral energy, selected by a per-layer energy threshold or by a global byte budget filled by water-filling, optimal for the continuous relaxation and empirically near-optimal for discrete rank allocation. Nothing is trained and no subject image is read, so the method applies to legacy and third-party checkpoints for which training-time adapters such as LoRA were never produced. The factors merge back into dense weights at load time, so serving runs at the uncompressed model's exact latency, whereas whole-model 8-bit and 4-bit quantization slow inference by 1.5-3.4 times. On the 30-subject DreamBooth benchmark, Delta-SVD matches the uncompressed model to within 0.01 DINO at 7-fold compression and keeps 98% of its fidelity at 33-fold compression. Among post-hoc baselines, only dense-delta quantization at 411 MiB matches it; below that size Delta-SVD dominates pruning, random-rank selection, and both whole-model and dense-delta quantization on the storage-quality frontier. The same holds on 84 diverse CustomConcept101 subjects, where a 9 MiB adapter reproduces the uncompressed outputs at paired DINO 0.77, and on a fully fine-tuned SD3.5-medium MMDiT, where a 531 MB adapter matches the uncompressed model to within 0.01 DINO.
comment: Accepted to ACML2026
♻ ☆ Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
Wenrui Zhou, Jiashun Liu, Sujie Hu, Bang Liu, Ling Pan
Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.
♻ ☆ Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 10.7% for the best competing WAM.
comment: 28 pages; Project page: https://huiwon-jang.github.io/FRED/
♻ ☆ In- and Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs for Simple Visual Planning Tasks
Yannic Neuhaus, Chanoknan Tanchotikul, Nicolas Flammarion, Matthias Hein, Francesco Croce
Integrating reasoning in (multimodal) large language models has recently led to significant improvement of their capabilities. However, generalization in reasoning models is still vaguely defined and poorly understood. In this work, we present an evaluation framework to rigorously examine how well chain-of-thought (CoT) approaches generalize in simple visual planning, specifically on a grid-based navigation task. The versatility of the task and its data allows us to fine-tune model variants using different input representations (visual and textual) and CoT reasoning strategies, and systematically evaluate them under both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test conditions. Our experiments show that the out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., to larger maps) is largely impacted by the format used for input maps and CoT chains. Surprisingly, we find that coordinate-based reasoning traces which combine text descriptions yield the best OOD generalization. Moreover, CoT reproducing the steps of the A* algorithm yields the state-of-the-art ID accuracy, and simple augmentation of the map solutions seen during training greatly boosts OOD results. Repeating the experiments with maps represented by coordinates yields similar results for another model family. Tests on structurally complex maps reveal a sharp performance drop when shortest solutions require many movement directions or turns. Additional fine-tuning on examples of directionally complex maps substantially recovers this performance. Finally, purely text-based models consistently outperform those utilizing image-based inputs, including a recently proposed approach relying on latent space reasoning.
♻ ☆ JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
Daniel G. P. Petrini, Davi Pincinato, Fabio Grassiotto, Pedro L. F. Prado, Alexandre F. S. Osorio, Raphael V. Ramos, Felipe Pamboukian
We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures
♻ ☆ Automated open-set multi-view seahorse re-identification from underwater photograph sequences
Tristan Fauvel, Sylvie Louisy, Patrick Louisy, Thomas Fauvel
Automated animal re-identification from photograph sequences can facilitate minimally invasive Capture-Mark-Recapture studies at scale. Yet, photographs taken during an observation session can vary greatly in quality, not always providing the necessary information for accurate re-identification. In this paper, we present new methods for open-set re-identification from image sequences. We train and evaluate taxonomic classification, sex determination and re-identification models on a dataset of 35,853 photographs of 473 individual seahorses observed in the wild. Combining the photographs of an observation improves all three tasks. For species and sex, a linear probe on DINOv3 embeddings classifies each photograph, and we average the logits over the photographs of an observation. For open-set re-identification, we retrieve candidate individuals with a fine-tuned MiewID descriptor, and weight each photograph by a learned relevance score. Local feature matching with ALIKED and LightGlue combined with a geometric check with RANSAC that keeps only the consistent matches then reranks the candidates. A logistic model estimates the probability that the individual is already in the gallery. A maximum a posteriori rule then chooses between the best-matching identity and a new individual. This method reaches a normalised accuracy of 0.91 when the gallery holds every past observation of each individual, and 0.82 when it holds only one.
♻ ☆ GOLD-SLAM: Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM
Weicong Zhang, Yuan Huang, Yu Zheng, Lin Chenxiao, Yingying Li, Lilong Fan, Liangdong Zhuang, Yufan Chen, Ruiping Liu, Junwei Zheng, Jiaming Zhang
Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. Compared with existing panoramic baselines, GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 5.56-9.10 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9-83.9%. To assess deployment feasibility on resource-constrained platforms such as UAVs, we evaluate an embedded configuration of GOLD-SLAM on a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), demonstrating online operation at the cost of reconstruction quality.
comment: The project repository is available at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/GOLD-SLAM
♻ ☆ OVOK: A Recursive Self-Improving Agentic Framework for Video-Based Articulated Robot State Estimation
Cheng Dai, Renkai Luo, Guanfeng Tang, Siming Li, Hao Zhao
Recovering articulated robot state from video supports metric spatial sensing for manipulation, scene reconstruction, and action planning. Yet the problem is ill-posed: different intrinsics, camera-to-robot poses, and joint angles can explain similar observations. Prior task-specific regressors typically assume known intrinsics, fit one robot through laborious data collection and robot-specific training, and still transfer poorly across scenes. Foundation models apply to any robot zero-shot, but their estimates have large errors. We present OVOK (One Video to Kinetics), a recursive self-improving agentic framework for this task. Under a human-authored protocol, an agentic initializer constructs robot-specific OVOK-4k; a proposer--executor--verifier loop then jointly evolves tools and executable workflows from feedback. Updated tools and workflows are accepted only when the verifier judges a positive improvement. The retained workflow is frozen for accurate inference. Experiments demonstrate that the evolved workflow achieves state-of-the-art results on DREAM-V and RoboKeyGen-V, delivering robust and accurate estimates.
comment: 24 pages, including appendix
♻ ☆ SynAVID: A Synthetic Audio-Visual Immersive Dataset of Dynamic Scenes
Jun Xu, Sujing Li, Chunhao Bi, Zhengxue Cheng, Ronghua Wu, Qunshan Gu, Li Song
Immersive scene modeling requires synchronized visual and auditory observations under changing viewpoints and scene conditions. Obtaining such observations and references for controlled scene changes remains challenging. We introduce SynAVID, a synthetic audio-visual immersive dataset comprising eight indoor and outdoor scenes. Each minute-scale episode combines fixed camera arrays and moving trajectories with synchronized, viewpoint-dependent binaural audio. Shared scene dynamics, sound-source events, and observer poses drive visual rendering and geometry-aware acoustic synthesis. We evaluate existing methods for visual reconstruction, binaural audio reconstruction, and audiovisual editing. Mixed-observation configurations generally improve visual reconstruction on fixed and moving test views, while transiently occupied and sparsely observed regions remain challenging. Methods rank differently on spectral, interaural, and perceptual audio metrics. Geometric and instance annotations expose uneven observation support and local Gaussian representations beyond aggregate scores. Paired references assess target edits and surrounding content, while controlled geometry changes produce listener-dependent acoustic responses. The project page is available at https://avery-xu.github.io/synavid-project/.
♻ ☆ HumanPhys: A Human-Centric Physical-World Perception Benchmark for Real-World Visual Reasoning
Yiming Zhang, Enzhi Zhou, Junan Lin, Dulan Zhou, Weiqiang Wang, Yuge Huang, Jian Liu
We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
♻ ☆ ReliaGuard: Reconstruction-Aware Watermarking for Source Attribution and Blind Edit Localization
Hailong Wang, Wuzheng Tan, Zixin Zhang, Xujun Fang, Fengjuan Gong
Generative image editing can reconstruct the background outside the requested edit, weakening spatial watermark evidence even when the source identifier remains recoverable. This creates an ambiguity for blind localization: a weak watermark response may indicate either an intended edit or background reconstruction. We propose ReliaGuard, a reconstruction-aware watermarking framework that addresses this ambiguity through reconstruction-stable evidence writing and coarse-to-fine blind reading. The writer aligns keyed feature responses in the protected image and its variational autoencoder reconstruction while preserving a frozen source-attribution channel. A quantization-aware projection bounds the distortion of the released eight-bit image. The reader combines keyed responses with image context to refine a base localization map, then integrates native-resolution detail with multiscale features to estimate the edit region. It is trained on paired observations before and after image processing and requires only the received image and key at inference. On 300 source images and 900 editing cases from three domains, ReliaGuard achieves intersection-over-union scores of 85.61% for complete editing outputs and 94.90% for locally spliced outputs at thresholds calibrated to a nominal 1% background false-positive rate on complete outputs. The former exceeds the strongest baseline by 45.02 percentage points, while decoded identifier-bit accuracy reaches 100% in both conditions. Across seven image-processing families, the corresponding localization scores remain 81.01% and 86.49%, with identifier-bit accuracies of 92.76% and 92.79%. These results show that reconstruction-aware writing and contextual reading can jointly support source attribution and edit localization under generative editing and subsequent image processing.
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Updated version
♻ ☆ Co-located Mobile AR from Brief Mutual Sightings of Users
Mohammad Rashid
Co-located augmented reality requires all devices to express virtual content in a common frame. ARKit and ARCore establish this frame by matching visual features of the room, so every device must first scan the same surfaces. In contrast, we propose a registration method based on brief mutual sightings of the users. Since devices align their vertical axis with gravity, two frames differ only by a yaw angle and a horizontal translation. When device A observes the user of device B at bearing $α$ while B observes the user of A at bearing $β$, the two lines of sight are antiparallel and the relative yaw is $α- β+ π$, without depth, markers or a commonly observed surface. A sighting is not forced and may last less than a second, which is especially useful in applications where users frequently view each other. Ranged sightings add point correspondences, and a server fits all devices under a Cauchy loss. Devices without depth sensors get dense depth from a point-map network (MoGe-2). In deployment, 85% of 4,613 iOS devices without LiDAR converged in a median of 24 s (81% without ultra-wideband ranging), against 87% of LiDAR devices and 66% of 3,048 Android phones. Depth arrived within 10 s in 84% of iOS sessions, when ARKit had found a wall in 32%. Its scale was within 2% of ARKit's wall planes but varied by 8% between frames, which thickened walls about fourfold; an offline per-frame correction reduced wall thickness from 27 to 17 cm on iOS and from 50 to 22 cm on Android. The converged frame still drifted by a median of 6° in yaw. Unlike map sharing, the method needs no scanning step, depth sensor or exchange of images, so a shared session can start on phones as soon as users see each other. The principle also applies to head-worn displays and to robots that observe one another. Future work will run the scale correction on-device and hold the frame once converged.

♻ ☆ TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.

In compact models targeting resource-constrained processors, such as microcontrollers, these remaining full-precision components determine the total memory footprint, severely limiting deployment efficiency and on-device feasibility. In this work, we introduce a fully ternarized Vision Transformer in which all weight matrices and normalization parameters are ternarized, while activations remain 8-bit (FTerViT). To this end, we introduce two novel operators: TernaryBitConv2d with per-channel scaling for patch embedding and TernaryLayerNorm. FTerViT is trained using knowledge distillation, followed by a lightweight quantization-aware recovery phase. On a matched DeiT-S backbone, FTerViT reaches 77.47% ImageNet-1K top-1 at 5.81 MB, +3.27 pp over TerViT. With the stronger DeiT-III-S backbone at 384x384 resolution, our ternary W2A8 model achieves 82.43% at 6.09 MB (~15x compression, -2.42 pp vs. FP32). This backbone- and resolution-advantaged result exceeds prior ternary ViTs by up to 8 pp. Finally, we demonstrate the first implementation of ternary vision transformers on a dual-core Xtensa LX7 microcontroller inside the ESP32-S3 system-on-chip. By deploying FTerViT-Small (based on DeiT-III-Small at 224x224 resolution, 5.81 MB), we achieve 79.64% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy.

Jie Song, Jun Jia, Wei Sun, Wangqiu Zhou, Tao Tan, Guangtao Zhai
Multimodal medical image fusion integrates complementary anatomical and functional information from different imaging modalities, providing richer image representations for clinical interpretation and assisted diagnosis. High-performance medical image fusion models are typically built upon medical images with high data sensitivity and security requirements, together with carefully designed algorithmic architectures. Collectively, these constitute intellectual property of significant value. As fusion results are circulated and reused in scenarios such as cross-institutional collaboration, traceable copyright protection and controlled authorization for these medical fusion assets are becoming increasingly important. However, existing multimodal medical image fusion models typically generate unprotected results and lack built-in copyright protection and authorization mechanisms. Conventional post-processing watermarking is independent of the fusion model, making it difficult for copyright protection to become an intrinsic capability of the model itself. To address this issue, we propose AMIF, the first Authorizable Medical Image Fusion model with built-in authentication, which integrates authorization access control into the image fusion objective. For unauthorized usage, AMIF embeds explicit and visible copyright identifiers into fusion results. In contrast, high-quality fusion results are accessible upon successful key-based authentication.

The threat is most acute for the photos people actually share, which have 10 megapixels or more and which current editors first downscale by a factor that the owner does not know. We propose SRIM, a protection that remains effective at every scale an editor may use, without knowing its preprocessing and at the same computational cost as standard expectation over transformation. SRIM covers the range of scales implied by the photo size with anchor scales and spends each optimization step on the scale where the protection is currently weakest. A spectral analysis shows that this worst-case protection degrades only logarithmically with the width of the range, a value that averaging over scales cannot reach. Extensive experiments on full-resolution photos and popular instruction-guided editors validate that SRIM gives the strongest protection, outperforming existing methods even with a quarter of their $\ell_\infty$ budget, remaining the strongest under input purification.

Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Language models can generate LEGO$^\circledR$ assemblies from text, but their builds often contain parts that collide or attach to nothing. The usual approach of rejecting and resampling invalid placements discards decoded tokens without guaranteeing a valid build. We present BriConstrain, a constrained decoding method that restricts a pretrained language model's next-token probabilities before sampling, steering it towards valid placements. Because the validity of a brick placement depends on the non-predetermined build state, it cannot be compiled into a fixed grammar and must be checked dynamically. However, checking the validity of a brick before sampling is challenging as the space of valid placements is combinatorially large and cannot be enumerated exhaustively. Our key idea is to narrow the search space by constraining how parts attach rather than which parts attach to each other. Concretely, given the model's predictions of the currently placed part, and the previously placed parent it wants to connect to, we constrain the model's choice of how they attach. This allows us to span the space of part attachments, using a precomputed geometric oracle, and to effectively filter out colliding options. With valid attachment candidates in hand, we bias the model's next-token distribution towards the remaining valid candidates. We evaluate our method on two LEGO$^\circledR$ formats and models: BrickNet, which annotates connectivity explicitly, and our proposed Implicit Connectivity LDraw Format (ICLF), which uses numeric values for placements and leaves connectivity implicit. Our method raises collision-free builds from 31% to 91% on BrickNet and from 15% to 65% on ICLF, and outperforms rejection sampling on both formats at about 60% of its decoding cost.

We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.

Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.

Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.

☆ From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution ICLR 2027
Hantao Hua, Jiming Su, Yonggang Che, Feng Zhu

Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. Human-facing text understanding systems are used to infer affect, moderate harmful content, and support socially sensitive decisions. However, Transformer predictions are difficult to audit because they are produced from high-dimensional hidden states that do not provide a compact, inspectable interface for human analysis or intervention. We introduce Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. Token representations are mapped into concept activations, filtered by learned gates, pooled into layer-level summaries, and exposed to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. The dimensions can be inspected through usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc concept names, and targeted concept interventions. We evaluate GCA on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. In the affective and safety-relevant classification settings, GCA learns comparatively low-redundancy and intervention-sensitive concept representations while retaining useful predictive performance. On toxicity detection, it remains close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline while enabling concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control. On GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces this gap. On AG News, GCA remains competitive with recent concept-based baselines, and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarifies the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction. Overall, GCA provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.
comment: Preprint. Includes supplementary appendices
☆ Evaluating Latent Knowledge Stability in Multimodal Large Language Models
Chuancheng Shi, Shangze Li, Wenhua Wu, Zifeng Cheng, Pengyang Shao, Fei Shen, Tat-Seng Chua
Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.
☆ Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards
Iliyan Zarov, Henry Course, Anthony Hartshorn, Ran Achiron, Louis Roche, Akshit Sinha, Chengxi Taylor, Ross Taylor
We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection. The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.
☆ What If Chinese Were Latinized? A Counterfactual Study of Input Representation, Tokenization, and Language Modeling
Zijie Zheng, Ej Zhou
If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer. We convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin and train superBPE tokenizers from scratch. The resulting Pinyin vocabularies not only exhibit expected homophone collisions, but also show approximately 10% higher fertility than characters. An alternative BPE configuration changes the relative fertility of the two representations. We further pretrain Llama-style models on Chinese characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall ZhoBLiMP minimal-pair accuracy. An exploratory phonological probe yields near-chance performance for both representations. The broader implication is that written input representations are not merely neutral encodings. Choices for representations affect language modeling and their downstream performances. Latinization never actually happened for Chinese, but other languages did, such as Hangul and Latin script replaced character in Korean and Vietnamese; the cost we measure is a guide to where modeling effort for those languages should concentrate.
☆ STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
Yi Zou, Zhuang Yan, Yudong Zhang, Xu Wang, Yang Wang
Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

☆ BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
Xiao Ma, Lin Li, Shiqing Wu, Wang Gao, Chuanbo Liu, Jianquan Liu
Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.
comment: Accepted at NLPCC 2026
☆ MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
Yifan Dai, Daili Hua, Bohan Zeng, Yuran Wang, Jialing Liu, Bozhou Li, Chengzhuo Tong, Yang Shi, Kai Zeng, Liu Yang, Xinyu Liu, Shujie Li, Yiyan Ji, Bingyin Mei, Yushuo Guan, Yuanxing Zhang, Fangcheng Fu, Wentao Zhang
Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

☆ Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
Bernard Muller, LaVonne Roberts
Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant. The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not. Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.

☆ When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
Akshata A Bhat, Daman Deep Singh, Niyati Chhaya
Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.
☆ Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
Mohamed Eltahir, Manar Eyad, Yara Alzahrani, Fatimah Albesher, Duaa M. Tahir, Tanveer Hussain, Naeemullah Khan
Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

☆ On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
Linhao Zhong, Bozhen Fang, Xuehao Wang, Zekai Luo, Liyang Li, Hourong Li, Chenchen Jing, Hao Chen
Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/
☆ Decision Models: An Introduction and Capability Evaluation
Rongtao Zhang, Mingjing Qi
Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need decisions that software can act on. Decision models provide these outputs through explicit types for choices, binary judgments, and policy scores. We evaluate the accuracy, output validity, and request latency of eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites. StartLux Instant achieves 95.3% overall accuracy, returns valid outputs on all 1,000 cases, and has a median request latency of 0.084 s. It reaches 99.4% on classification and routing and selects the correct response on all 100 tool-selection cases. The highest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations is 97.1%. These results show how a typed decision service can support fast, programmatic decisions and why its suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.
☆ Implementation of Machine Translation for the Uzbek Language Based on Transformer Models
Mukhammadjon Musaev, Mannon Ochilov
This research focuses on building a machine translation system for the Uzbek language using transformer models such as T5 and mT5. Because of the limited data and the complexity of the Uzbek language, we collect, preprocess and augment data to create a strong Uzbek-English parallel corpus of about 3 million sentence pairs. The models are fine-tuned for optimal translation performance, and we use the BLEU score to evaluate the results. This study shows that our approach significantly improves upon older methods and helps promote the Uzbek language in the digital world.

☆ ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
Chanseul Cho, Dongwoo Kim, Noori Bae, Seungjae Moon, Seongsu Lee, Youngmin Ro
Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.

☆ ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
Ahmed Maher Khafaga Shehata, Mohammed Nasser Al-Suqri, Nour Eldin Mohamed Elshaiekh Osman, Faten Hamad, Yousuf Nasser Alhusaini, Ahmed Mahfouz
The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

Mark Farinas, Alesandra Garcia, Maria Reyes, Jethro Nueva, Nawaf Qureshi, Mahmoud Elsaadany, Shokry Shamseldin
In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.

Yi Liu, Changqing Ai, Peijie Dong, Xiankun Lin, Yongkang Yang, Zhezheng Hao, Xilin Xia, Hande Dong, Qiang Lin, Qiang Xu
Runtime skills can improve agents' problem-solving capabilities by providing procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging. However, these benefits reach only a minority of users, as most do not proactively invoke skills in practice. We argue that such generalizable procedures should become part of the model's capabilities rather than remain optional external add-ons, making them directly available without explicit skill loading. To this end, we present SkillCore, a data pipeline and supervised fine-tuning recipe for internalizing generalizable skills. We transform real agent trajectories by removing skill-loading scaffolding while preserving the task context and subsequent agent actions, thereby supervising direct execution without external skill content. To preserve access to task-specific skills that provide genuinely external information, we mix these scaffold-removed trajectories with a small proportion of skill-native trajectories that preserve supervision for skill invocation. On a held-out skill-free evaluation, SkillCore improves task completion quality over the base Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-72B models by 54.4% and 24.8%, respectively, while preserving task-specific skill invocation on a separate probe and general coding performance on SWE-bench Verified.
