Hamdy Mubarak, Anas Madkoor, Ehsaneddin Asgari, Majd Hawasly
Automated understanding of handwritten Arabic student essays remains challenging due to script complexity and high variability in children's writing. We introduce ArEssays, a large-scale dataset of authentic essays from primary to secondary students across Egypt, with both verbatim transcriptions and linguistically corrected versions. We benchmark 34 vision-language and OCR models, including fine-tuned systems, and find large performance gaps on real student handwriting. We release the dataset, training pipelines, and results to support research in Arabic OCR, document understanding, and educational NLP.
☆ Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
Henry Castillo, Yanchen Liu, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, Dylan Hadfield-Menell
Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.
☆ ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks NeurIPS 2026
Jiawei Gu, Linjie Li, Yiming Liu, Yunzhuo Hao, Huichen Wang, Guanzheng Chen, Zhichao Peng, Luxin Xu, Xinyu Zhang, Li Luo, Disen Lan, Zican Hu, Mingyang Song, David Valente, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Yafu Li, Ganqu Cui, Zhengyuan Yang, Qizhe Xie, Yejin Choi, Ranjay Krishna, Yu Cheng
People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://thinkmorph.github.io/ssl/
☆ RightDiff: Learning Generative Reward Models to Judge by the Right Differences
Qiyuan Chen, Hongsen Huang, Jiahe Chen, Renjie Hua, Hongxia Xu, Chuan Ren, Jian Wu
Generative reward models typically rely on generic query-level rubrics or unconstrained rationales, overlooking the fact that pairwise preference is driven by response-specific differences. Moreover, optimizing solely for outcome correctness encourages models to exploit superficial shortcuts such as verbosity and formatting, triggering rationale drift. To address this, we propose RightDiff, which structures pairwise evaluation into an evidence-grounded evaluation trajectory executed in a single autoregressive generation. RightDiff explicitly discovers contrastive differences between candidates, categorizes them into material or immaterial factors, and induces pair-specific rubrics before final adjudication. To train this process without post-hoc rationalization, we synthesize demonstration data via response-isolated prompts and optimize the reward model with a difference-alignment reward regularized by budget-constrained one-to-one matching and multiplicative gating. RightDiff achieves state-of-the-art preference modeling performance on RewardBench and RM-Bench, surpassing all open-source reward models and leading proprietary LLM judges. Downstream, it provides reliable supervision for direct preference optimization on Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval while effectively resisting length shortcuts.
☆ Making Evaluation Explicit Is Not Enough: Supervising the Evaluation Process in Generative Reward Models
Qiyuan Chen, Yuze Zhao, Jiahe Chen, Hongsen Huang, Hongxia Xu, Yingda Chen, Jian Wu
Generative reward models (GRMs) make language-model evaluation more explicit by generating critiques, rubrics, or intermediate analyses before predicting a final preference. However, explicit evaluation does not necessarily imply a reliable evaluation process: under outcome-only supervision, a model may reach the correct final preference while producing weak or unsupported intermediate judgments, turning the evaluation into a post-hoc rationalization. We introduce STEP-GRM, a framework that directly supervises the intermediate evaluation process of rubric-based GRMs. In addition to conventional preference supervision, STEP-GRM provides structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, encouraging the model to learn not only the correct final preference but also a more reliable process for reaching it. Extensive experiments show that STEP-GRM achieves strong performance on standard reward-modeling benchmarks while improving the consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations. Moreover, reward signals produced by STEP-GRM lead to better downstream policy optimization, demonstrating that more reliable evaluation processes can translate into practical gains beyond reward-model accuracy.
☆ ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models
Xiangwei Wang, Jianyuan Lin, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge
First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. Open-weight LLMs are competent software engineers, but they sometimes fail at tasks they are otherwise able to do. Often it is not a failure of reasoning. It is a few small missteps over a long trajectory (repeating a step that has already failed, or declaring the task done while a requirement is still unmet) that make the difference. Correcting this calls for a surgical weight update that steers the model toward the right actions without interfering with its reasoning. Such updates, typically learned with LoRA adapters, are often too small to survive merging into a released checkpoint. In our BF16 release, the median weight change is only 1.5% of a single rounding step, and merging loses roughly two thirds of the update's norm. When the same adapter is merged into the mixed FP8/NVFP4 release of the same model, 93% of the update disappears. Instead of increasing the size of the update, we directly train on the surviving part. We introduce merge-aware fine-tuning. Standard LoRA rounds the merged weights to the storage format only at export, so the loss never sees the rounded weights. We instead round the sum of base weights and adapter update to the release format at every training step, keeping the vendor's quantization scales, and compute the loss on these weights. The forward pass matches the serving engine numerics, and the gradient passes straight through the rounding, so the model we train is the model we ship. The loss optimizes only the model's actions and keeps its reasoning close to the base model. Applied to Nemotron-3.5, the recipe improves agentic coding in both the BF16 and the NVFP4 release, by up to 8.4 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and we publicly release both models.

☆ Grounding Language Models in Revealed Audience Behavior

The same 8B model is right about half the time when asked which headline readers will click and 86.5% of the time when grounded in the clicks; the strongest prompting we tried only matches a text classifier; a grounded 0.6B model beats every prompted frontier model in our runs; and whether the clicks are fitted as counts or as shares makes no detectable difference in a pre-registered test. Where: across four behaviors, grounding wins where the text carries the signal (short-video likes, +20 points on 200 pre-registered videos), only ties an asked model given the reader's history (news clicks), and nothing text-only gets far from chance on watch time. Code, adapters and run outputs will be released.

To test this, we use linear mode connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language adapters, evaluating on three tasks. We find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected, whereas mathematical reasoning (Math) pairs are not, indicating that basin geometry is task-dependent. Such disconnection in Math is ``local'' rather than global. A small target-language task sample, applied only to the English adapter's language encoding or semantic composition layers, is enough to repair it. Cross-lingual generalization is also factorizable into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each supplied separately from a cheaper signal. English task data routed to the composition layers and an unlabeled target-language corpus routed to the language encoding layers each alleviate it on their own for nearly every pair. Composition is the more influential of these, and it needs no target-language data. Together, these results suggest that cross-lingual generalization decomposes into language-specific and language-agnostic components in parameter space. This decomposition offers a practical route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.

☆ Subliminal Learning Crosses Modalities

Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.

Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.

A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

☆ HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling

Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

In an exploratory comparison on the same images, no common threshold on any trained encoder reproduced the adults' narrow-to-broad gain (at most 66.67 vs. 76.43 percentage points). ♻ ☆ Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin

Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.

Dynamic-tree methods such as EAGLE-3 perform well under greedy decoding via deterministic top-K expansion and global pruning. However, in stochastic decoding (T>0), this mechanism collapses the draft distribution into one-hot probabilities, causing a severe drop in acceptance rate. This creates a dilemma: dynamic-tree methods sacrifice stochastic sampling to preserve context-aware topology, while static-tree methods preserve stochastic sampling with context-agnostic structures. This coupling makes direct injection of randomness challenging due to the resulting stochastic process. We resolve this by decoupling these roles: RheoSampling assigns a token sampled from the draft distribution a proxy probability for tree expansion and pruning alongside its true sampling probability for verification. Specifically, we inject a sampled token among the deterministic top-K slots and treat it with different probabilities during construction and verification, making RheoSampling the first dynamic-tree method with both context-aware top-K construction and stochastic sampling while maintaining losslessness. An OT-based verification strategy and a sparse draft mechanism ensure that theoretical gains translate into practical efficiency. This framework may provide a template for analyzing stochastic tree structures.

In this paper, we propose a unified perspective that casts tree-based verification as a conditional OT problem. Our key insight is that vertical dependencies can be abstracted through prefix acceptance probabilities, which act as dynamic scaling factors to actively guide horizontal draft selection. Based on this principle, we introduce UniVer, a verification algorithm that jointly optimizes across tree levels by composing local optimal transport plans under prefix constraints. We prove that UniVer remains lossless and achieves the optimal acceptance rate under the proposed conditional framework. Extensive experiments across different tasks and models demonstrate that UniVer improves acceptance length by 4.2% to 8.5% over standard recursive rejection sampling without replacement, while maintaining exact distributional alignment with the target model.
