♻ ☆ CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
Ilia Badanin
We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.
♻ ☆ Beyond Aggregate WER: In-domain Adaptation, Learner Speech, Code-Switching, and Speaker Attribution in Online Spanish Learning Classrooms
Olga Kellert, Samhitha Harish, Johnatan E Bonilla, Nemika Tyagi, Phanos Kareen, Nelvin Licona-Guevara
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly supplies transcripts for educational NLP, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns, and speaker attribution. We compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR configurations on held-out sessions of online L2 Spanish interaction between L1 English learners and their instructors and tutors. Because English is the learner's shared first language, the interactions contain Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate (CER), WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate (DER). We also adapt Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data. MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Domain match proved more important than data volume: Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus, where learner speech and code-switching are embedded in instructor--learner interaction. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech. The findings demonstrate the value of condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched data for bilingual educational ASR.
comment: 15 pages, 9 Tables, 2 Figures
♻ ☆ MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
Cheng Siong Chin
Marine and offshore engineering knowledge is scattered across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, but remains small by pretraining standards. We examine how far parameter-efficient adaptation can take a lightweight domain model on a workstation-class device. Starting from OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we trained two LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training on one NVIDIA DGX Spark took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second. The first used next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. Of 13,879 source documents, 7,069 remained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter to remove cross-domain lexical collisions. Validation loss fell from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. After the continuation adapter drifted off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, we trained an instruction adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs: 114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages. Loss was applied only to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts, hand-scored for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the base model, continuation adapter, instruction adapter and instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 81. The retrieval score reflects a corrected index-leakage issue. A paired test supports the instruction-tuning gain but finds no retrieval benefit on this set. Accuracy remained low: 14/40 without retrieval and 16/40 with it. A second evaluation used prompts from passages excluded from both instruction-data splits, addressing selection leakage in round one. It confirmed the instruction-tuning gain (p=0.0001 and p=0.0002) and found that retrieval significantly helped the base model, but not the instruction adapter.
comment: 4 figures, 10 pages
♻ ☆ TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
Guofeng Tong, Xu Zhang, Guangliang Yu, Haiqiang Wang, Guannan Cong, Xing Guo, Yang Zhou, Jingjing Duan, Shuang Li, Feng Shi, Hualei Liu
On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.
♻ ☆ Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models ICML 26
Siyan Zhao, Zhihui Xie, Mengchen Liu, Jing Huang, Guan Pang, Feiyu Chen, Aditya Grover
Knowledge distillation improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by compressing the knowledge of a teacher LLM to train smaller LLMs. On-policy distillation advances this approach by having the student sample its own trajectories while a teacher LLM provides dense token-level supervision, addressing the distribution mismatch between training and inference in off-policy distillation methods. However, on-policy distillation typically requires a separate, often larger, teacher LLM and does not explicitly leverage ground-truth solutions available in reasoning datasets. Inspired by the intuition that a sufficiently capable LLM can rationalize external privileged reasoning traces and teach its weaker self, we introduce On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), a learning algorithm where a single LLM acts as both teacher and student with different contexts. The teacher policy conditions on privileged information (e.g., verified reasoning traces) while the student policy sees only the question; training minimizes the per-token divergence between these distributions over the student's own rollouts. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving superior token efficiency compared to reinforcement learning methods and better performance over off-policy distillation methods. Code repo: https://github.com/siyan-zhao/OPSD.
comment: ICML 26, code: https://github.com/siyan-zhao/OPSD
♻ ☆ A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle EMNLP 2026
Zehao Lin, Xixuan Hao, Renyu Fu, Shaobo Cui, Kai Chen, Chunyu Li, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong
The emergence of writable, cross-session persistent memory in LLM agents introduces a qualitatively different threat landscape from conventional input-centric security concerns, characterized by three properties: persistence, statefulness, and propagation. To systematically characterize this landscape, we propose a Memory Lifecycle Framework that organizes attacks, defenses, and their cross-phase dependencies along two axes: six lifecycle phases (Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share & Propagate, Forget & Rollback) and four security objectives (Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability, Governance). This analysis in turn exposes the need for explicit security requirements at the system level, motivating Verifiable Memory Governance (VMG), a framework of five architectural primitives for specifying and evaluating auditable, recoverable control over memory state within declared system and threat-model boundaries. Our analysis motivates integrating provenance, versioning, and policy-aware retention with retrieval and execution defenses to support auditable prevention, containment, and recovery across the lifecycle.
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Expanded version of the EMNLP 2026 paper. Adds evidence on persistent representations, skill memory, authorization changes, and recovery. Table 4 compares lifecycle security claims and their evaluation conditions
♻ ☆ Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
Jiapeng Pei, Yuhang Yao, Sitan Liu, Hanxin Chen, Hao Li, Guogeng Li, Jiapei Liu, Ruijie Chen, Hongshan Lin, Shangding Gu, Yang Mo, Tianyu Shi
Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

♻ ☆ Towards Understanding On-Policy Distillation through the Lens of Test-Time Scaling
Xinmu Ge, Zizhuo Zhang, Yu Huang, Jianing Zhu, Lin Yuan, Wanli Gu, Weichang Wu, Weiran Huang, Bo Han, Xiaolu Zhang, Jiangchao Yao
On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as a promising post-training technique for enhancing LLM reasoning. Under the reverse KL objective, the idealized optimum of OPD aligns the student distribution with that of the teacher. When the teacher consistently outperforms the student, this naturally suggests that OPD should yield broad improvements over the pre-OPD student. However, do such improvements extend across the entire range of test-time sampling budgets? In this work, we revisit this expectation through the lens of test-time scaling by varying the sampling budget $K$ and evaluating performance with pass@$K$. Across multiple settings, we observe two distinct patterns: OPD can improve pass@$K$ at both small and large sampling budgets, but it can also improve small-budget performance while reducing large-budget pass@$K$. We show one condition that guarantees such a reversal and an idealized reverse KL counterexample where it occurs even when the teacher has higher accuracy on every problem. To choose between two candidate teachers at a target sampling budget, we propose the \textit{Teacher Advantage Score at $K$} (TAS@$K$), which can be computed before OPD training to predict which teacher will lead to a larger improvement in pass@$K$. Across three domains and thirteen benchmarks, the ordering predicted by TAS@$K$ agrees with the observed pass@$K$ improvements of the resulting OPD models in 83.6\% of experiments, providing a useful signal for teacher selection at the target pass@$K$.

♻ ☆ DEBATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Evaluating Opinion Dynamics in Role-Playing LLM Agents NeurIPS 2026
Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Ruixuan Tu, Chengtao Dai, You Li, Smit Vasani, Binwei Yao, Michael Henry Tessler, Sijia Yang, Dhavan Shah, Robert Hawkins, Junjie Hu, Timothy T. Rogers
Modeling opinion change through social interactions is important for understanding polarization, misinformation, and societal conflict. Recent work simulates opinion dynamics with role-playing LLM agents (RPLAs), but multi-agent simulations often display unnatural group behavior (e.g., premature convergence) and lack empirical benchmarks for assessing alignment with real human group interactions. We introduce DEBATE, a benchmark for evaluating the authenticity of opinion dynamics in multi-agent RPLA simulations. Its three-round design makes each participant's public interaction history complete and traceable. DEBATE contains multi-round public messages and private Likert-scale beliefs from U.S.-based participants across 107 topics. The dataset covers 2,788 participants in 697 groups, enabling evaluation at the utterance and group levels. We instantiate "digital twin" RPLAs with seven LLMs and evaluate across two settings: Next Message Prediction and Full Dynamics Simulation, using stance-based opinion-dynamics metrics. In zero-shot settings, RPLA groups exhibit strong opinion convergence relative to human groups. Across group-generalization tests with unseen participant groups and topic-generalization tests with unseen discussion topics, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3.5-4B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 improves stance-based alignment and reduces excessive convergence, bringing RPLA group convergence closer to that observed in the corresponding human groups, though discrepancies in opinion change and belief updating remain. The dataset, benchmark website, and codebase are publicly available.
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Track on Evaluations and Datasets
♻ ☆ Probing the Prompt KV Cache: Where It Becomes Dispensable ACL 2027
Vinayshekhar Bannihatti Kumar, Manoj Ghuhan Arivazhagan, Disha Makhija, Rashmi Gangadharaiah
Prior KV cache compression schemes empirically demonstrate that the prompt cache can be dropped or summarised during decoding with little accuracy loss, indicating that it is partly redundant. We ask when and what kind of redundancy, i.e., at which layers, after how many decoding steps, and in what form can the prompt span KV cache be replaced without breaking the task. A controlled splice intervention swept over layers and decoding steps shows this redundancy is about form rather than content. Replacing the upper layer prompt span KV cache with KV cache from a chat template scaffold with empty user content or filler tokens recovers near clean accuracy, while zeroing the entire prompt KV collapses accuracy. The dissociation replicates across the Qwen3, Gemma 3, and Llama 3 model families of varying sizes on multiple datasets. A serving implementation of this technique reduces KV memory by $15.4\%$, supports $18\%$ more HBM-constrained concurrent requests, and improves throughput by $13$-$21\%$.
comment: Accepted in the proceedings of EACL 2027 (Main)
♻ ☆ Frozen Scenes, Shifting Winners: Configuration Fragility in Text-to-3D Evaluation
Anson Y. Lam, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
Can a text-to-3D leaderboard change when every generated scene stays fixed? We audit this question for rendered-image evaluation, where camera settings and caption wording become part of the measurement protocol. Across 300 frozen scenes from six generators, we vary eight render and caption factors for 19 alignment evaluators plus one perceptual-quality control, then test four targeted scene degradations. Peak configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 19/19 alignment evaluators, with prompt-bootstrap lower bounds above 1 for 19/19. Rankings are more stable than scores, yet 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration. Pairwise protocol margin envelopes show which comparisons keep their direction across the tested settings. Selected pairs have opposite pointwise intervals, but no reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search. Thus the observed winner changes are descriptive, not confirmed changes in generator superiority. Sensitivity remains separate: no evaluator exceeds 71% tie-adjusted directional discrimination on layout scrambling, and a preregistered blinded human study classifies part of the configuration variance as metric artifact. The audit separates score stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity, and recommends reporting (generator, score, card ID) with protocol-dependent comparisons and selection-aware uncertainty.
comment: 33 pages, 6 figures
♻ ☆ Verify Before You Generate: Sketch-Guided Efficient Motion-Planning for Video Generation WACV 2027
Yidong Huang, Zun Wang, Han Lin, Dong-Ki Kim, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Jaehong Yoon, Yue Zhang, Mohit Bansal
Recent video generation approaches increasingly rely on planning intermediate control signals like object trajectories to improve temporal coherence and motion fidelity. However, these methods mostly employ single-shot plans that are typically limited to simple motion instructions, leading to suboptimal motion quality, or iterative refinement which requires multiple calls to the video generator and incurs high computational cost. To address this trade-off, we propose SketchVerify, a training-free framework whose key insight is to verify motion plans using lightweight video sketches before invoking the expensive video generator. This lightweight planning space enables efficient comparison of multiple candidate trajectories and bounded iterative refinement before a single final video-generation pass. Given a prompt and a reference image, SketchVerify samples multiple candidate trajectories and renders each as a lightweight video sketch by compositing the moving objects over a static background. A vision-language verifier then ranks these sketches according to instruction alignment and visual motion consistency, allowing unsuitable trajectories to be rejected before full video synthesis. The motion plan is iteratively refined until a satisfactory one is identified, then passed to a trajectory-conditioned generator for final synthesis. Experiments on WORLDMODELBENCH and PHYWORLDBENCH demonstrate consistent improvements in instruction following and temporally coherent, visually plausible motion. Using the same ATI-14B generator, SketchVerify improves the aggregate WorldModelBench score from 7.71 to 8.71. Compared with full-video iterative refinement, it achieves a 13.1x planning-stage speedup and a 3.6x end-to-end speedup.
comment: Accepted by WACV 2027, website: https://sketchverify.github.io/
♻ ☆ MatLoom: Layered Text-to-Material Generation in a Compact Program Space
Anson Y. Lam, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
Material generation should produce not only an appearance, but also the rules that construct it. We introduce MatLoom, a compact, layer-oriented language for text-to-material generation with pretrained language models. Each program composes alpha-masked layers whose shared spatial expressions define coverage and physically based rendering (PBR) channels, making dependencies between patterns, color, and relief explicit. A standalone interpreter evaluates the program into material maps, while the source retains named fields and layer parameters for subsequent authoring. Without task-specific fine-tuning, our pipeline uses parser-guided repair and preview-based critique to revise material designs, then searches noise seeds while keeping each candidate's remaining source fixed. On a curated benchmark of 141 prompts evaluated with six backbones, our best-performing configuration achieves higher mean scores than three diffusion baselines on all four flat-layout prompt-alignment metrics, and the margin persists on seven of the eight metric-layout cells under feasible equal-budget selection including best-of-10 sampling with the same quick scorer, with staged CLIPScore a statistical tie. A per-metric oracle bound over the same ten samples, which requires test labels, narrows the judge margins to 6.1 points flat and a staged statistical tie. Its initial programs already exceed all three baselines on mean BLIPScore, before critique or seed search. Retained programs have a median length of 21 lines when pooled across backbones. In a blind four-way comparison involving 30 participants and 20 prompts, our renders receive 59.2% of choices, compared with 19.3% for the most-preferred baseline. Compact executable programs thus offer a way to generate prompt-aligned materials while retaining their construction as part of the asset.
comment: 43 pages, 9 figures
♻ ☆ Compute Optimal Tokenization
Tomasz Limisiewicz, Artidoro Pagnoni, Srini Iyer, Mike Lewis, Sachin Mehta, Alisa Liu, Margaret Li, Gargi Ghosh, Luke Zettlemoyer
Scaling laws enable the optimal selection of data amount and language model size, yet the impact of the data unit, the token, on this relationship remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate how the information granularity of tokens, controlled by the compression rate (i.e., average bytes of text per token), affects scaling trends. We train 988 latent tokenized models (BLT) ranging from 50M to 7B parameters that enable setting the desired compression rate. This flexibility allows us to study the role of compression rate well beyond 4.57 bytes per token obtained with a popular BPE tokenizer. Our experiments reveal that in compute-optimal configurations, model parameter counts scale proportionally to data size measured in bytes, not in tokens as commonly perceived (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Furthermore, we discover that the optimal compression rate differs from the one obtained with BPE and decreases with compute. These findings generalize to both latent and subword tokenization, as well as to languages other than English, guiding language model developers on tokenization scheme selection for maximal compute efficiency.
♻ ☆ RAG Makes Guardrails Brittle? Investigating Robustness of Guardrails under RAG-style Contexts
Yining She, Daniel W. Peterson, Marianne Menglin Liu, Vikas Upadhyay, Mohammad Hossein Chaghazardi, Eunsuk Kang, Dan Roth
With the increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs), ensuring the safety of LLM systems has become a pressing concern. External LLM-based guardrail models have emerged as a popular solution to screen unsafe inputs and outputs, but they are themselves fine-tuned or prompt-engineered LLMs vulnerable to data distribution shifts. In this paper, taking Retrieval Augmentation Generation (RAG) as a case study, we investigate how robust LLM-based guardrails are against additional information embedded in the context. Through a systematic evaluation of 3 Llama Guards and 2 GPT-oss models, we find that inserting benign retrieved documents flips the judgments of input and output guardrails in around 11% and 8% of cases respectively, with the majority of these flips (72% and 64%) reversing previously correct decisions. We further analyze the effect of each component in the augmented context: retrieved documents, user query, and LLM response. Two tested mitigations reveal that the robustness gap is not easily closed. These results expose a context-robustness gap in current guardrails.
♻ ☆ AhaBench: Do Agents Turn Experience into Reusable Insights? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Continual Learning
Zerui Cheng, Jiawei Xu, Huacan Chai, Jiayang Sun, Pramod Viswanath, Maxm Pan
Solving a task, even from a worked example, does not make an agent any better at the next one. As agents move from single tasks to long collaborations with people, turning experience into reusable insight becomes the capability that separates a tool from a collaborator that improves over time. AhaBench is a benchmark for this kind of continual learning. It simulates three patterns of long human-AI collaboration and holds a later test fixed while varying the experience before it: in Aha-Puzzle, the agent questions a partner who knows the answer to a new mystery after solving earlier ones; in Aha-Euler, a person teaches a computation and the agent applies it to new inputs; in Aha-Vending, the agent runs a delegated business for a simulated year. The learning mechanism is left open, so memories, skill libraries, and weight updates can be compared under common rules against a baseline of fixed-weight agents that see their experience in context. Our results show that today's frontier agents are not yet continual learners. Earlier Aha-Puzzle solutions help some models, most clearly Qwen 3.6 Plus, which gains +12.57 points over attempts on the same stories without earlier episodes, yet every model scores far below what it reaches with hints. On single-step Aha-Euler tasks, the same model solves 94.0% of requested held-out inputs when taught with an explanation and code but 6.0% when given only the question and answer, counting unanswered attempts as incorrect. In incident-free Aha-Vending operation, Doubao Seed 2.0 Pro ends the year at +495 USD, yet its profit averaged over the year is -10 USD because it recovers late. Exploring without help, reconstructing a method, and sustaining productive operation remain open problems, and AhaBench provides the paired tests a learning method must pass to solve them.
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 150
☆ Non-penetrating World Models
Yuhang Dai, Yinwei Wu, Ziyue Lin, Han Ji, Xingyi Yang
We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.

Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. ☆ SUPERVISE: A Unified Framework for Standardized and Reproducible Superpixel Evaluation
Julien Walther, Rémi Giraud, Michaël Clément
Image segmentation into superpixels is a widely used technique in computer vision, with a large body of work developed over the years. Yet, its evaluation remains poorly standardized, as methods are compared under heterogeneous protocols, across inconsistent scale ranges, and with redundant or misaligned metric subsets. In this work, we introduce SUPERVISE (SUperpixel PERformance VISualization and Evaluation), a unified and reproducible benchmark that addresses these longstanding inconsistencies. Built on a scale-normalized protocol based on interpolation over the actual number of generated superpixels, SUPERVISE enables fair and consistent cross-method comparisons. We leverage this standardized framework to conduct the first large-scale statistical analysis of 20 evaluation metrics across 7 datasets and 31 methods, revealing strong inter-metric correlations and significant redundancy that challenge common evaluation practices. These findings provide empirical support for reporting a compact set of representative metrics. SUPERVISE is released as a lightweight, modular framework built on precomputed shared label maps, making large-scale reproducible evaluation accessible to the community. All code, label maps, and evaluation results are publicly available at: https://github.com/waldo-j/supervise
☆ RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
Junying Wang, Yijin Guo, Yalun Wu, Ziheng Jiao, Farong Wen, Qihang Yan, Wenzhe Li, Ye Shen, Qi Jia, Chunyi Li, Zicheng Zhang, Guangtao Zhai
Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. To address VLM fragility, we further propose RoSci-Agent, a framework that employs a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline to vet premises before reasoning. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. RoSci-Agent achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the evaluated standalone VLMs. RoSci-Bench gives the multimodal reasoning community a common test of when models answer, request clarification, or reject a scientific question.

☆ Quantitative Measurement of Pavement Distress based on Vehicle Camera and Perspective Correction
Sike Wang, Yizhou Lin, Shuo Li, Yi Jiang, Chengcheng Tao
Using image data is becoming an important method for highway agencies to automatically evaluate pavement conditions. However, most studies focus on improving detection accuracy rather than obtaining quantitative measurements, such as the length or area of pavement distress. Although field camera calibration can provide such measurements, it is impractical for large volumes of onboard images collected from different vehicles. This study develops a method to quantitatively measure pavement distress directly from in-vehicle camera images without on-site camera calibration. A quadrilateral region of interest is first identified based on lane detection and used to construct a perspective transformation matrix for image correction. Size correction is then performed using the proportions of road markings in the image and a specified scale, which also enables estimation of the actual width of the selected region. The corrected images are subsequently processed using object detection algorithms to obtain quantitative distress measurements. The proposed method can efficiently perform perspective correction for images collected by the same vehicle camera with minimal manual effort. The measured pavement patch lengths show a trend consistent with pavement friction data. By calibrating vehicle cameras using only image information, this study enables quantitative pavement distress detection without additional field experiments. The approach provides a practical solution for processing large volumes of vehicle-camera data, particularly as connected vehicles generate increasing amounts of uncalibrated roadway imagery.
☆ PAWS: A Parametric Model of Canine Pose and Shape
Theo Wieland, Zala Žgank, Silvia Zuffi, Ylva Mellbin, Elin Hernlund, Hedvig Kjellström
We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape. We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.
☆ VeilGS: Solving Darkness as a Veil of 2D Basis Maps over Retinex 3DGS
Mohab Kishawy, Chengzhou Tang, Shahram Shirani, Jun Chen
In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

☆ When Are Images Needed in Multimodal Machine Translation? Text-Only Routing for On-Demand Visual Context
Xinyu Wang, Yingfeng Luo, Yuxin Gao, Anxiang Ma, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao
Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.
☆ Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
Zhenxuan Fan, Zhuoya Wang, Yuqian Yuan, Wenqiao Zhang, Juncheng Li, Jun Xiao, Siliang Tang, Yueting Zhuang
Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
☆ CanopyFormer: Attention-Guided SegFormer for Explainable Forest Cover Segmentation
Dhinanjaya Fernando, Dinura Ginige, Kalana Lakshan, Chanupa Gurusinghe, Lasana Pahanga, Dileesha Manamperi, Thimira Sahan, Sandareka Wickramanayake
In transformer segmentation models, attention is usually visualized after training rather than supervised. Although attention supervision has been explored for natural images and driving scenes, aerial forest segmentation typically uses attention only as an architectural component and evaluates interpretability qualitatively. We present CanopyFormer, an attention-guided SegFormer-B0 that uses an Attention Consistency Loss to align attention with the ground-truth forest mask, encouraging attention to focus on canopy regions. Since SegFormer uses spatial-reduction attention, we adapt Gradient-weighted Attention Rollout by restricting it to the final encoder stage, where the attention matrix is square. We introduce Average Attention-Mask Overlap (AAMO) to measure attention alignment and incorporate a deletion test to evaluate faithfulness. On 5108 images, our method increases AAMO from 0.0334 to 0.7476, approximately 22 times the vanilla SegFormer-B0 result, with a modest decrease in Dice score from 0.8743 to 0.8577. The deletion test reveals that improved alignment does not necessarily translate into improved faithfulness: removing the most-attended 25% of patches reduces the forest score by 12.1%, compared with 33.0% when removing random patches. Attention supervision introduces no additional inference cost, although double backpropagation makes each training step 2.6 to 2.8 times slower. The attention alignment improvement also generalizes to a second dataset, LoveDA. Additionally, a Boundary Refinement Module provides no consistent Dice improvement and reduces AAMO, while mean squared error substantially outperforms Kullback-Leibler divergence as the attention loss.

☆ GeoScaffold: From Latent to Realized Geometry in Collaborative Detection
Kang Yang, Yance Fang, Gaochen Cui, Xiaoqiang Jin, Deying Li, Yongcai Wang
Most collaborative 3D detectors fuse bird's-eye-view (BEV) features from connected vehicles and roadside infrastructure to aggregate complementary observations. Although modern communication, alignment, and fusion pipelines encode rich latent geometry in the fused BEV features, the standard readout pipeline inherited from single-agent detectors, i.e., anchor scoring, box decoding, and non-maximum suppression (NMS), does not fully exploit these geometric cues. We empirically identify and quantify this gap on UrbanIng-V2X. Collaboration improves localization at about two-thirds of positive anchors, yet when NMS resolves two overlapping collaborative boxes of one object, it keeps the better-localized box less than half of the time. A key cause is a supervision mismatch: classification scores are trained only for foreground-background discrimination, so nothing in training requires them to rank boxes by localization quality. To address this limitation, we introduce GeoScaffold, a lightweight training-only auxiliary objective. It predicts a foreground mask at each positive anchor, i.e., the cells of a grid over the anchor that lie inside the ground-truth box, to supply the dense spatial supervision that the seven-dimensional box code leaves implicit. Its loss, added to the detection loss, updates the encoder and fusion modules through the fused BEV and trains the detector toward a better-localized box at every positive anchor, including the top-scored one. The auxiliary head is removed at inference, preserving the original detector architecture, communication logic, and inference cost. GeoScaffold raises AP@0.5 and AP@0.7 by 0.98 and 0.55 points on average across all 11 fusion methods on the UrbanIng-V2X validation split, with gains extending to most methods on an unseen intersection and to all ten methods that produce detections on V2V4Real.

☆ Beyond Sample Hardness: Adaptive Data Selection through Learning Dynamics
Hai Gan, Suorong Yang, Guang Li, Baile Xu, Furao Shen
Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Specifically, we track per-sample loss dynamics using exponential moving averages (EMA) to obtain three complementary signals that capture current learning difficulty, ongoing learning improvements, and potential degradation. To accommodate evolving training dynamics, we introduce Adaptive Metric Fusion, a contextual bandit-based mechanism that dynamically adjusts the relative importance of these signals based on training feedback. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures
☆ MoHA: Model-Conditioned Harness Adaptation for Long-Video Agents
Jianghan Chao, Wenhui Tan, Hang Su, Qiuyu Tian, Tanxiao Li, Bingzi Zhang, Zequn Liu, Ruihua Song, Yingce Xia
Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA.
comment: 24 pages, 3 figures. Code: https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA
☆ Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio Sánchez-Benítez, Christian Chwala
GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

☆ SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
Anqi Li, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds. Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives. We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision. At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels. A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed. On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3x speedup and retains 98% at 2.5x. Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
comment: 16 pages, including supplementary material. Anqi Li and Kai Liu contributed equally
☆ Seeing Is Not Steering: Where Verifiable Reasoning Can Enter an End-to-End Driving Planner
Gautam Kumar Jain, Atharva Mahindrakar, Shubham Phoolari, Ignacio Alvarez, Carsten Markgraf, Constanze Hungar, Christoph Lauer, Julian Staehler
Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
☆ Segment Everything, Materialize Nothing: Exact Streaming Inference for Many-Class 3D Segmentation
Fabian Isensee, Jakob Wasserthal, Lalith Kumar Shiyam Sundar, Maximilian Rokuss, Moritz Langenberg, Constantin Ulrich Harsy, Stefan Michael Happold, Klaus H. Maier-Hein
Whole-body segmentation tools such as TotalSegmentator and MOOSE split more than 100 classes across five or six networks. The reason is memory. Standard 3D inference, as implemented in nnU-Net and MONAI, holds a logit for every class and voxel, on the working grid and again on the scanner's grid. For a median whole-body CT at 125 classes, that is 76 GB. We show that this memory wall lies in what inference materializes, not in the task, and remove it without approximation. Every step after the network is local along one axis, so its outputs can be streamed through a ring one patch thick. The classification head commutes with blending and resampling, so the ring carries the network's features instead of the class logits. Memory thus no longer grows with classes times volume, and the label map on the scanner's grid stays exact. This holds for any model with a pointwise affine head, without retraining. Many-class models, previously impractical, become deployable. One model trained on all classes matches or slightly exceeds the toolkits' five or six specialists in segmentation quality and runs 5.8-15x faster end to end, with 3.2-7.6x less RAM and under 8 GB of VRAM. We provide the method as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator and MOOSE. The code is part of nnU-Net (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet), and unified models for both toolkits will be released.
☆ Points, Not Pixels: Keypoints, Masks and Oblique Geometry for Floating-Roof Tank Fill Estimation from Overhead Imagery WACV 2027
Mohd Shahid Kaleem, Mohd Hozaifa Khan, Maaz Khan
The floating roof of an oil storage tank rests on the stored liquid, so its depth below the rim measures how full the tank is. In optical overhead imagery, this depth appears only as the crescent shadow the rim casts on the roof, often a few pixels wide. Thin shadows are difficult to measure at overhead-image resolution, and nadir-based height conversions introduce errors in oblique views. Under a local affine camera, roof depth determines the rim-to-shadow displacement through the sun and camera geometry. We regress the boundaries as sub-pixel keypoints and invert this relation with a closed-form estimator that models oblique views. Available public tank datasets do not label roof position, so we introduce SynTank-25k, 24,987 physically based renders with exact roof, shadow and camera geometry. Using the oblique estimator, the keypoint pipeline reduces fill error by $22\%$ relative to the segmentation baseline on SynTank-25k. On shadows narrower than $6\text{ px}$, its error is also lower than that obtained by converting true binary masks. Our oblique estimator reduces the error of the nadir formula elevenfold at the steepest views. On 6,558 real NAIP tank crops defined by bounding boxes, about half of the fill estimates pass internal consistency checks; NAIP has no fill labels. Data and code will be released.
comment: Accepted to Workshop on Computer Vision for Earth Observation Applications at WACV 2027
☆ Automating Multi-View Quality Assessment of 3D Annotation Layouts
Hongyi Yang, Jinao Wu, Yanwei Zhang, Shengwen Fu, Haibin Ling, Bingyao Huang, Jingwei Qu
Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

☆ Sketch2TikZ: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Converting Hand-Drawn Sketches to Executable TikZ BMVC 2026
Shubham Paliwal, Arushi Jain, Monika Sharma, Manasi Patwardhan
Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.
comment: Accepted Main Track at BMVC 2026
☆ Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
Ignazio Gallo, Mattia Gatti, Leonardo Sgroi, Darwin Castillo, Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona, Nicola Landro
Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above the best of nine imaging arms (0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, returns the same audit outcome from a different confounder. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

☆ GameScrub: Learning HUD Removal from Real Gameplay with Recovered Targets
Mohammad Areeb Qazi, Yiyan Hu, Yanan Wang, Xuezhi Liang, Xin Li, Fan Yang, Xin Gao, Guangyi Liu
Gameplay videos are a rich source of experience for learning virtual-world dynamics, yet their frames contain heads-up displays (HUDs) that follow interface rules rather than scene dynamics. Removing HUDs would make this footage directly usable for learning world dynamics. However, training a removal model requires paired clips with and without HUDs, whereas real recordings contain only HUD-overlaid footage. Existing work synthesizes pairs by compositing HUD graphics onto HUD-free footage, requiring a separately curated clean corpus and producing HUDs that only approximate real ones. Models trained on such pairs leave 40 to 50% of real HUD elements untouched. We instead recover pseudo-clean targets directly from real recordings by inpainting HUD regions with a pretrained video diffusion model. Preventing HUD traces from leaking into recovered targets is challenging because latent video autoencoders mix information across mask boundaries. Our training-free recovery pipeline, GameScrub-Data, pre-fills HUD regions with flow-guided background estimates before encoding, excludes HUDs from scene conditioning, and confines restoration to masked regions through pixel-space compositing. The resulting pairs train GameScrub, a video diffusion removal model that handles diverse HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images. On the in-the-wild Game2World benchmark, GameScrub achieves an artifact-adjusted removal score of 71.95, compared with 57.86 for the strongest reference-free GameCleaner configuration, and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%. These results demonstrate that real recordings with recovered targets can support effective HUD removal, advancing HUD-free gameplay data for world models and controllable video generation.
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures
☆ When Visually Rich Documents Meet Multi-Vector Retrieval for Region-level Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Xu Yuan, Liangbo Ning, Yujuan Ding, Qing Li, Wenqi Fan
Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.
☆ From Tokens to Pixels: Training-Free Guided Upsampling of Frozen CARL Features for Hyperspectral Imaging
Dominik Fromme, Ellen Markowski, Tim Streckert, Jörg Thiem
Camera-agnostic foundation models such as CARL map spectral images from arbitrary sensors into a shared feature space, but deliver their features only on a token grid at one eighth of the input resolution. The usual bilinear interpolation blurs material boundaries over about one token and rounds off corners. We investigate how much spatial accuracy image-guided upsampling recovers for frozen CARL features without training the encoder or the upsampler. We compare joint bilateral upsampling (JBU), a guided filter and the pretrained AnyUp, each with the hyperspectral image or an RGB rendering as the guide. A hyperspectral ColorChecker dataset acquired specifically for this study, with model-independent reference geometry measured to sub-pixel precision, serves as the evaluation benchmark. JBU with the hyperspectral guide raises the Boundary IoU from 13 to 67 % and reduces the effective edge width of the features from 38 to 4 px, close to the resolution of the raw spectra. To investigate this setting, we capture approximately \textbf{40 hours of real-world 8K panoramic UAV video} and construct \textbf{PanoUAV-Track} through temporal clip extraction, target annotation, and the integration of simulated sequences. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,895 sequences, 507,961 frames, and 2,872 annotated objects, covering real-world daytime and nighttime scenes alongside simulation, and supporting both visual and language-based target specification. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack)}, a geometry-aware tracking framework combining latitude-adaptive search and seam-aware periodic sampling. The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.

Public availability gating further reduces encrypted computation by removing branches determined by publicly known task and owner availability without altering predictions. Overall, CoGITAtion enables gaze model reuse, efficient privacy-preserving deployment, and robust inference under incomplete owner availability while retaining interpretable gaze representations.

For each candidate, we predict the displacement and distance from shared spatial locations to the nearest points in its completion. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.

The accurate detector reads decoded frames with a video language model and is too expensive for every chunk, so our guard reads hidden states the generator has computed already and spends a cheap score on deciding when to call it. On 599 streams from a distilled causal generator the undefended model shows 46.25 harmful frames of 81. The video model on every chunk leaves 0.91 frames at 80.1 scored per benign stream, and the same model triggered by our guard leaves 2.35 at 5.3. Spending that budget at random leaves 37.20 frames, so the gain is in the ordering, and a frame detector in the same role gives up almost six, so the judging stage must read the chunk as a clip. The ordering is worth more as the stream lengthens, and the guard carries to a second system. An independent guardrail model agrees with our oracle at $κ=0.74$, and a blinded audit by 50 participants puts its precision at 96.1% and recall at 82.8%. Warning. This paper contains examples of generated content that some readers may find disturbing or offensive in nature.

☆ EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
